extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for peer reviewers evaluating NLP research submissions to conferences/journals (e.g., ACL/EMNLP/ARR), focusing on anti-patterns to avoid and constructive/operational reviewer norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: "The paper is not SOTA"
rubrics_metrics.description: "The paper is not SOTA" — failure to set new state-of-the-art is not by itself a reason to reject; many useful contributions are not best-on-benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not recommend rejection solely because a paper does not achieve a new state-of-the-art on a benchmark. Evaluate the paper on the merit of its claims, contributions, methodology, clarity, and reproducibility. Consider other kinds of contributions such as analysis, diagnostics, datasets, or robustness even if they are not top-performing on benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: "This is not novel / I have seen this idea before"
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is not novel / I have seen this idea before" — without specific citation showing prior identical work, a vague feeling of familiarity is not a substantive critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming lack of novelty, provide precise citations and explain how the cited work is the same or why the current submission adds nothing beyond it. Vague assertions of 'I've seen this' are insufficient; reviewers should identify specific prior work and describe overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: "The improvement is too small / not significant"
rubrics_metrics.description: "The improvement is too small / not significant" — small effects are not necessarily uninteresting; statistical significance and effect-size discussion are required of the reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing small improvements, quantify the effect-size and discuss statistical significance and practical importance. Distinguish between incremental but meaningful advances and claims that are unsupported. Ask for proper statistical analysis rather than dismissing results based on subjective magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Not enough experiments / I would have run X more experiments"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not enough experiments / I would have run X more experiments" — reviewers should ask only for experiments necessary for the claim, not for additional experiments they personally find interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between 'blocker' experiments necessary to support the paper's central claims and 'wishlist' experiments that are optional. Request additional experiments only if they are necessary to validate core claims; otherwise suggest them as optional future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: "This is not deep learning / not neural" (methodological prejudice)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is not deep learning / not neural" (or, conversely, "this is just neural networks") — methodological prejudice rather than substantive evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rejecting or downgrading work because it does not use a fashionable method. Judge methods by appropriateness, rigor, and evidence, not by whether they match a preferred paradigm. Provide concrete reasons why a method's assumptions or evaluation are insufficient if raising methodological concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: "This is not interesting to me"
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is not interesting to me" — reviewer's personal taste is not a discipline-relevant ground for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate personal taste from community relevance. If a reviewer believes the topic is of limited interest, they should justify that claim with evidence about scope, applicability, or novelty rather than relying on subjective boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: "The paper is not well written"
rubrics_metrics.description: "The paper is not well written" — presentation defects, unless catastrophic, should be raised as fixable concerns, not rejection grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out specific presentation problems (unclear figures, missing definitions, poor organization) and indicate whether they are fixable in revision. Avoid using 'bad writing' as a catch-all reason for rejection without specifying how writing impedes understanding of the technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Wrong venue / not for ACL"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wrong venue / not for *ACL" — fit complaints should be flagged to the area chair, not used as a default reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paper appears misaligned with the venue, explain why and notify area chairs rather than issuing an automatic rejection. Consider whether the paper's scope matches workshop/short/long paper formats and calibrate recommendations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: "You did not cite my paper" (coercive citation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended anti-pattern: "You did not cite my paper" — coercive citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand citation of the reviewer's own work without demonstrating relevance. Recommend citations only when they materially relate to the paper's claims, and suggest specific relevant references rather than coercive self-promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: "This requires expensive compute" as reject reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended anti-pattern: rejecting because "This requires expensive compute" — penalizes low-resource groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider resource constraints of authors and the research context. Avoid rejecting work solely because it uses costly compute; instead evaluate whether the compute-related claims are adequately supported and whether experiments are necessary for the claims made.

rubrics_metrics.name: "This is not in English" as a critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended anti-pattern: criticizing work for not being in English (or expecting English-only references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful about language and cultural biases. If language quality impedes comprehension, point to specific issues and suggest remediation. Do not reject work simply for using or citing non-English sources when they are appropriate to the research context.

rubrics_metrics.name: "The dataset is too small" without domain context
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended anti-pattern: "The dataset is too small" without considering domain constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dataset size relative to domain norms and feasibility. Small datasets may be intrinsic to certain tasks or languages; ask for justification if necessary, but avoid blanket dismissal of small-dataset work.

rubrics_metrics.name: "You should have used model X" (method preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended anti-pattern: "You should have used model X" — preference, not necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insist on specific models or architectures unless there is a clear methodological reason they are necessary to validate claims. Suggest alternative models as possible comparisons, and explain why they are essential if requesting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Your method is not theoretically motivated" for empirical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended anti-pattern: "Your method is not theoretically motivated" when empirical contributions are valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that empirical contributions can be valuable without strong theoretical motivation. If theoretical grounding is expected for the venue or claim, explain why; otherwise evaluate the empirical rigor and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite specific prior work when claiming lack of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Cite specific prior work when claiming lack of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting that a contribution is not novel, reviewers must provide exact citations and explain the overlap. This enables area chairs and authors to assess novelty claims fairly and avoids vague rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish "blocker" from "wishlist" comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Distinguish 'blocker' from 'wishlist' comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label reviewer requests as 'blocker' (must be addressed to validate the paper) or 'wishlist' (nice-to-have improvements). This clarifies priorities for authors and ACs and prevents demands for unnecessary additional work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider resource constraints of the authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Consider resource constraints of the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of compute, language, or data access limitations authors may face. Suggest feasible alternatives and avoid demanding experiments or resources that are unrealistic for the authors' context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge contributions before raising concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Acknowledge contributions before raising concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start reviews by noting the paper's strengths and contributions to provide balanced feedback. This practice reduces adversarial tone and helps authors and ACs see the reviewer's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer constructive alternatives for criticised choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Offer constructive alternatives for any criticised choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pointing out a flaw, propose practical alternatives or fixes (e.g., different evaluation, baseline, or analysis) rather than only stating negatives. Actionable suggestions are more helpful during rebuttal and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the same standards across submissions in the batch
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Apply the same standards across submissions in the batch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrate scoring and expectations consistently across papers you review to avoid unfair advantage or bias. Be explicit if a paper receives different treatment due to venue type (workshop/short/long).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate review expectations to the venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Calibrate to the venue (workshop / short / long paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust expectations for scope, evaluation, and depth according to the submission type. For example, workshops or short papers may legitimately have narrower scope or preliminary results; reflect that in recommendation and required changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the author response during rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive norm: Engage with the author response during rebuttal, not stand on initial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisit your review in light of authors' rebuttal and clarify or update concerns. Use rebuttal content to resolve misunderstandings and to indicate which requested changes are still blockers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the Responsible NLP Research Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational norm (ARR): Reviewers must complete the Responsible NLP Research Checklist as part of their review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill out the checklist to surface ethical, societal, data, and reproducibility considerations. Use it to flag responsible-research issues and to guide review comments; see the Responsible NLP Research Checklist for items to check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard scoring axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational norm (ARR): Reviewers must use the standard scoring axes: Soundness, Excitement, Reproducibility, Ethical Concerns, Overall Recommendation, Confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide scores (and supporting text) on each axis. 'Soundness' evaluates methodological correctness; 'Excitement' covers novelty/impact; 'Reproducibility' examines clarity and artifact availability; 'Ethical Concerns' addresses harms/risks; 'Overall Recommendation' synthesizes accept/reject; 'Confidence' indicates reviewer certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide actionable revision suggestions for low scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational norm (ARR): Reviewers must provide actionable revision suggestions for any below-threshold score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any axis receives a below-threshold score, list concrete steps authors can take to address the deficiency (e.g., additional analyses, clarifications, baseline comparisons). Actionable suggestions help area chairs, authors, and meta-reviewers judge whether revisions could rescue the paper.
